intro: A league is a paper agreement before it is a season of games. In 1788 a London cricket club printed laws that other clubs chose to follow. In 1920 football team owners met in a Canton, Ohio, car showroom and wrote rules for themselves. In 1921 a Chicago judge became baseball's first commissioner and banned eight players a jury had acquitted.

School sport has its own papers. School boards meet in public, courts decide what can happen in a public stadium, and voters approve bonds that pay for fields. Booster clubs raise money privately, so some Friday night dollars are easy to trace and others are not.

In this unit you will read league founding records, commissioners' rulings, court cases and public records laws. You will be able to explain who writes a league's rules, who can see a school's sports money, and back up your answer with named dates and documents.
bigQuestion: Who writes the rules for a league or a school team, and who has the right to see how its money is used?

a single official chosen by a league's owners to govern the sport and punish wrongdoing
the belief and rule that athletes should not be paid to play

moving a club down to a lower division because of poor results

test.q: Which private club became the keeper of cricket's laws after 1787?
test.why: The MCC issued revised laws in 1788 and kept them for more than two centuries.

test.q: What was the Jockey Club's strongest punishment?
choices: A fine paid to the king
Removal from the Hall of Fame
test.why: Warning off banned a person from racecourses under the club's rules.

test.q: What did Kenesaw Mountain Landis do after the Black Sox were acquitted in 1921?
choices: Banned all eight from baseball for life
test.why: Landis banned the eight players the day after the jury found them not guilty.

test.q: Where was the league that became the NFL founded in 1920?
test.why: Owners met in Ralph Hay's showroom in Canton, Ohio.

choices: Northern clubs wanted to pay players for lost work time
A dispute over the size of the ball
test.why: Northern clubs wanted broken-time payments, which the Rugby Football Union refused.

test.q: Which year began tennis's Open Era?
test.why: Major tennis opened to professionals in 1968.

test.q: What limit did the 1936 NFL draft put on college players?
choices: They had to join a union
They had to play in Chicago
Each could negotiate with only the team that picked him
test.why: The draft gave one team the right to sign each chosen player.

test.q: Which statement about the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League is accurate?
choices: It was founded by Philip K. Wrigley in 1943
It was founded in Canton in 1920
It admitted Black players from its start
It had no rules about conduct
test.why: Wrigley founded the league in 1943, and it set rules on appearance and conduct.

test.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in American Needle v. NFL in 2010?
choices: The NFL is a single entity
NFL teams are separate businesses when they license logos
test.why: The unanimous Court applied antitrust law to NFL teams' licensing.

test.q: Why did the Santa Fe pregame prayers count as the school's speech?
choices: The prayers were printed in a newspaper
They were given at school events, on school property, over school equipment, under a school policy
test.why: The Court relied on the school setting, equipment and policy.

test.q: What was the result in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District in 2022?
choices: The coach's quiet postgame prayer was ruled protected, 6 to 3
test.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 that the coach's prayer was private speech.

test.q: Why does Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA matter for high school sport?
choices: It said a state association of mostly public schools acts as the government
test.why: The 2001 ruling made such associations follow constitutional limits.

test.q: Which law lets a person in Illinois request a school district's spending records?
choices: The Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act
test.why: The Illinois FOIA of 1984 lets anyone request public records.

test.q: What did the Hartzell v. Connell ruling of 1984 say about school activity fees in California?
choices: They conflicted with the promise of free public education
test.why: The California Supreme Court held activities are part of free public education.

test.q: What does the Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act require, and whom does it leave out?
choices: Colleges report athletic money by men's and women's teams; high schools are not covered
High schools report profits; colleges are not covered
Booster clubs report gifts; schools are not covered
Pro leagues report salaries; colleges are not covered
test.why: EADA of 1994 covers colleges only; no federal law requires high school reports.

write.prompt: Should a public school district publish how much money its Friday night games bring in and spend? Argue your answer using at least three documents from this unit, such as the Illinois Freedom of Information Act (1984), the Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act (1994), Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA (2001) or Hartzell v. Connell (1984).
tips: Name each law, case or record you use and give its year.
Explain what the document says before you explain what it means for your argument.
Separate what is public money from what a private booster club controls.
Answer the strongest argument on the other side with a fact.
Use the unit's terms, such as transparency, disclosure and state actor.
